You are auditing Android/Kotlin AI-agent "skill" files for the "Jetpack Compose UI & state" topic across up to three source repos that are being merged into ONE Claude Code plugin. When multiple skills auto-trigger on the same code, contradictory guidance is a real defect.

Read the FULL content of every SKILL.md in these directories, plus any references/*.md files inside them (use Glob or Bash 'ls -R' first to discover reference files):

- [ahmed] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/everything-claude-code-mobile/skills/jetpack-compose/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)

- [chris] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/skills/skills/compose-state-deferred-reads/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)
- [chris] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/skills/skills/compose-state-hoisting/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)
- [chris] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/skills/skills/compose-state-holder-ui-split/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)
- [rcosteira] /Users/oleksandr.priadko/Documents/StudioProjects/sub/android-skills/plugins/android-skills/skills/compose/  (read SKILL.md AND any references/*.md inside)

Produce:
1. contradictions — cases where two sources give ACTUALLY OPPOSING advice on the SAME specific technical point (not merely different depth or wording of the same principle). Name both sources (labels: "ahmed" / "chris" / "rcosteira"), state each claim, and cite evidence (file path + the specific lines/quote).
2. bugs — code that is broken, will not compile, or is technically WRONG (e.g. catches and swallows CancellationException, loses state across config change, references undefined symbols, wrong plugin/order). severity: critical | major | minor. Cite the file + evidence.
3. depthComparison — which source is most detailed/actionable here and why.
4. uniqueValue — what each source covers that the OTHERS DO NOT (worth keeping regardless of who dominates).

Be precise; cite real file content. Do NOT invent contradictions where sources only differ in depth — that is the most common false positive. Set cluster="compose".

- adaptive: Instructions to make or update an app's UI so that it adapts to different Android devices including phones, tablets, foldables, laptops, desktop, TV, Auto and XR. It includes how to handle different window sizes, pointing devices (such as mouse) and text entry devices (such as keyboard) using the Compose MediaQuery API. It also covers multi-pane layouts using Navigation3 Scenes, adaptive UI components (such as buttons) with varying target sizes, and adaptive layouts (including navigation areas - nav rails and nav bars) using the Compose Grid and FlexBox APIs.
- agp-9-upgrade: Upgrades, or migrates, an Android project to use Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) version 9. Do not use this skill for migrating Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) projects.
- android-cli: Provides instructions for installing and using the `android` CLI. The `android` command-line tool is a critical tool for Android development and helps you create new Android projects, run Android apps on devices, manage and interact with Android virtual devices (including screenshots and UI inspection), manage Android SDK components, look up official Android documentation, and discover and install official Android skills.
- android-intent-security: Best practices for Android Intent security. Use this skill when auditing component configurations in AndroidManifest.xml activities, services, receivers) or source code handling incoming Intents (getIntent, getParcelableExtra) to prevent Intent Redirection and unauthorized access.
- appfunctions: Analyzes Android apps to identify key user workflows for AppFunctions such as creating a note, playing media, or sending an automated or AI agent triggered message, voice commands, or system shortcuts, without needing to open the app UI. Generates Kotlin code to expose these workflows to the Android system, allowing agents to discover and execute them on-device. Also refines KDoc documentation to ensure AI agents correctly understand and use the provided functionality.
- camerax: Provide technical guidance for Android camera development with CameraX. Use when implementing camera features, handling asynchronous recording lifecycles, wiring low-level hardware interop using CameraX, or integrating ML Kit or Media3 effects.
- display-glasses-with-jetpack-compose-glimmer: Provides guidelines for developing projected Android XR apps for display glasses using the Jetpack Compose Glimmer UI toolkit. This skill covers foundational Glimmer design principles, workflows for implementing Jetpack Compose Glimmer, and interaction models for the glasses form factor. Use this skill to build an Android XR Augmented Experience app with Jetpack Compose Glimmer that adheres to the Glimmer design system for optimized glasses styling.
- edge-to-edge: Use this skill to migrate your Jetpack Compose app to add adaptive edge-to-edge support and troubleshoot common issues. Use this skill to fix UI components (like buttons or lists) that are obscured by or overlapping with the navigation bar or status bar, fix IME insets, and fix system bar legibility.
- engage-sdk-integration: Helps developers integrate, debug, and resolve Play Engage SDK implementation issues. Use when adding Engage SDK support, generating publishing code, mapping data classes to entities, or fixing SDK-related errors.
- migrate-xml-views-to-jetpack-compose: Provides a structured workflow for migrating an Android XML View to Jetpack Compose. This skill details the step-by-step process, from planning and dependency setup, to theming and layout migration, validation and XML cleanup. Use this skill when you need to migrate an XML View to Jetpack Compose in an Android project. It solves the problem of converting the UI of a legacy XML View into modern, declarative Compose components while maintaining interoperability.
- navigation-3: Learn how to install and migrate to Jetpack Navigation 3, and how to implement features and patterns such as deep links, multiple backstacks, scenes (dialogs, bottom sheets, list-detail, two-pane, supporting pane), conditional navigation (such as logged-in navigation versus anonymous), returning results from flows, integration with Hilt, ViewModel, Kotlin, and view interoperability.
- perfetto-sql: Translates natural language data intents into syntactically valid Perfetto SQL queries and executes them against a local trace file. Use this skill to extract slice, thread, or memory data from Android Perfetto traces using trace_processor.
- perfetto-trace-analysis: Analyzes Perfetto traces to find the root cause of latency, memory, or jank issues in Android apps. Use when the user provides a Perfetto trace file and asks any question, ongoing investigation, or open-ended request to analyze its contents.
- play-billing-library-version-upgrade: Use this skill when upgrading or migrating an Android project from any legacy Google Play Billing Library (PBL) version to the latest stable version of PBL.
- r8-analyzer: Analyzes Android build files and R8 keep rules to identify redundancies, broad package-wide rules, and rules that subsume library consumer keep rules. - styles: Use this skill to integrate the Jetpack Compose Styles API into an Android project. This skill guides you through upgrading dependencies, setting up component themes, making custom components styleable, and migrating existing layout properties to use unified styles. Migrate custom design system components, replace hard coded parameters with Style attributes, and use Modifier.styleable for interaction states.

This includes the androidx.wear.compose.material3, androidx.wear.compose.foundation, and androidx.wear.compose.navigation3 libraries. Also working with core components such as AppScaffold, ScreenScaffold, and TransformingLazyColumn, and core Wear OS concepts such as ambient mode. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- core:architecture-ports: Apply ports & adapters (hexagonal) and clean-architecture rules when designing or reviewing how modules depend on each other — the dependency rule (domain imports no framework), repositories that hide storage, constructor dependency injection, structural interfaces/Protocols over inheritance, single-responsibility services, and DTOs across boundaries instead of ORM rows. Use when adding a service, repository, adapter, port, or handler; when wiring dependencies; when a domain module starts importing a framework/ORM/HTTP/cloud SDK; or when a file mixes business logic with I/O. Do NOT use for pure language-syntax style (types, formatting), test authoring, or security/authz review — those have their own skills.
- core:documentation: Guidance for writing and maintaining project documentation that stays accurate — keep one source of truth and link instead of duplicating, update docs in the same change as the code they describe, co-locate context with the code it explains, maintain a code-to-docs mapping so changes know which doc to touch, and never leave scratch files. Use when adding or editing README/architecture/integration docs, deciding where a piece of documentation belongs, reviewing a PR that changes behavior but not docs, or cleaning up stray notes/TODO files. Do NOT use for API reference auto-generated from code comments, or for code-style/testing rules.
- core:fail-fast: Apply fail-fast error handling — raise immediately on missing or invalid required values instead of returning null/defaults, never swallow exceptions in empty catch blocks, and use typed/custom error classes with actionable context. Use this skill when writing or reviewing error handling, validation, config/parameter reading, try/catch or try/except blocks, or when a defect surfaces far from its cause (works then breaks weirdly later). Trigger keywords — silent fallback, default value, swallowed exception, empty catch, error handling, defensive coding, guard clause. Do NOT use this skill for designing immutable data models (use immutability) or for forward-compatible unused parameters (use forward-compat-slots).
- core:forward-compat-slots: Apply the forward-compatible reserved-injection-slot convention — a constructor or function parameter prefixed with underscore AND typed optional is an intentionally-unused dependency slot kept so future callers can inject it without touching every call site. Use this skill when adding a dependency to a base class or shared signature that not all implementations use yet, when a composing facade must pass the same dependency uniformly to sub-services, when reviewing an unused parameter, or when deciding whether to delete vs keep an unused argument. Trigger keywords — unused parameter, reserved slot, forward compatibility, optional dependency, _logger, _param, injection slot. Do NOT use this skill for general immutability (use immutability) or fail-fast error handling (use fail-fast).
- core:immutability: Minimize mutability — default domain types to immutable, derive new state with copy-on-write instead of mutating in place, never mutate function arguments, and keep a pure functional core with side effects pushed to a thin imperative shell. Use this skill when designing data models, value objects, or state-transition logic; when reviewing code that mutates shared state, reassigns variables, or mutates passed-in arguments; or when separating business logic from I/O. Trigger keywords — mutable state, in-place mutation, copy-on-write, immutable, frozen, readonly, value object, functional core, shared state bug. Do NOT use this skill for error-handling/fallback decisions (use fail-fast) or for reserved unused parameters (use forward-compat-slots).
- core:pr-authoring: Apply evidence-based pull-request authoring practice — keep each change small (~100-300 lines of substantive change) and single-concern, link the issue so your tracker auto-updates, and follow your team's chosen PR workflow and merge style well. This skill presents the trade-offs of mono-PR vs stacked PRs and squash vs merge-commit rather than mandating one (record your team's pick in .claude/rules/team-conventions.md). Use this skill when opening a PR, sizing or splitting a change, naming a branch, writing a PR description, or deciding mono vs stacked. Trigger keywords — open a PR, pull request, branch name, PR description, split this change, change size, mono PR, stacked PR, squash, merge strategy, rebase. Do NOT use this skill for reviewing someone else's PR (use pr-review) or for commit-message wording alone.
- core:pr-review: Apply evidence-based code-review practice when reviewing a pull request or diff — calibrate review depth to the change's risk and blast radius, raise one finding per concern, classify each on a Required/Nit/Question severity ladder, and shape each comment as problem-grounded-in-the-diff then why-it-matters then a concrete fix. Use this skill when reviewing a PR, reading a diff, writing review comments, deciding review depth, triaging which findings block merge, or dispatching per-concern review passes. Trigger keywords — review this PR, code review, review the diff, review comment, severity, required vs nit, blocking finding, reviewer. Do NOT use this skill for authoring/sizing your own PR (use pr-authoring) or for running a specific language's linter/typechecker.
- core:secure-coding: Apply OWASP-based secure-coding rules when writing or reviewing code that handles authorization, secrets, logging, external input, persistence, network calls, or mobile local storage — server-side deny-by-default authz on every object/property/function, no hardcoded secrets (centralized store + rotation), never logging secrets/tokens/PII, validate-and-encode all external input, and mobile OS key stores with no plaintext local storage and TLS. Use when adding an endpoint/handler, an auth or ownership check, a logging statement, a DB or shell query, a config/secret read, an IAM policy, or any mobile data-at-rest code. Do NOT use for architecture/layering design or pure language-style/type rules — those have their own skills. Trigger keywords — SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, IDOR, path traversal, insecure deserialization, hardcoded secret, secret in logs, PII leak, sanitize, encode, deny-by-default authz, input validation, TLS, certificate pinning, Keychain, Keystore, clipboard/screenshot leak, key store.
- core:spec-implement: Orchestrate a tiered generator-verifier loop to implement a tightly-specified change cheaply — a strong-tier orchestrator writes the spec and rules, dispatches the cheap-tier executor agent to generate the code, then dispatches the matching strong-tier review agent to verify it, looping until the verifier is clean. Use when you have a SMALL, well-specified, mechanical implementation task (scaffold a component to a schema, boilerplate to a contract, stubs to a spec) and want to route generation to a cheap model while keeping verification strong. Trigger keywords — implement to spec, scaffold, generate to contract, model routing, cheap generate strong verify, generator-verifier, tiered agents. Do NOT use for ambiguous/design work (do it yourself on the strong model), for trivial one-liners (a single strong pass is cheaper than orchestrating), or for pure review with no generation (use pr-review).
- core:testing-behavior: Guidance for writing and reviewing automated tests that catch real bugs — test observable behavior through public APIs, verify resulting state instead of mock call sequences, write tests that survive refactoring, judge suite strength by mutation rather than coverage %, and treat flaky tests as defects. Use when writing unit/integration tests, deciding what to assert, reviewing a test file or PR's tests, debugging a flaky or brittle test, choosing mocks vs fakes, or interpreting a coverage report. Do NOT use for language-specific test-runner setup (pytest/jest/XCTest config) or for non-test code style.
- kotlin:android-architecture: Native-Android app architecture (Google's recommended layered architecture) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android app/feature module code (androidx.*/android.* imports, Activity/Fragment/Service/ViewModel, an :app or :feature module). Covers the UI/domain/data layers and one-way dependency direction Data <- Domain <- UI; single source of truth (the SSOT owns a data type, exposes it immutably, is its only mutator); unidirectional data flow (state down, events up); keeping app logic out of short-lived OS-owned Activities/Fragments/Services; and confining Context/framework classes behind your own abstractions for testability. Triggers — UI/domain/data layer, ViewModel, repository, single source of truth, SSOT, unidirectional data flow, UDF, Activity, Context. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); this is the layering overview, so for depth use android-ui-layer / android-data-layer / android-modularization / jetpack-compose, and for plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-data-layer: Native-Android data layer (repositories + data sources) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android repository, data source, Room/Retrofit/DataStore class, or DI wiring in an app/feature module. Covers the repository as the data layer's only public API (other layers never touch data sources directly); naming (DataType+Repository; DataType+Source+DataSource e.g. NewsRemoteDataSource); one single source of truth per type (offline-first local DB preferred); suspend for one-shot and Flow for streams; immutable exposed models; main-safety via withContext(ioDispatcher) where Dispatchers.IO IS correct (unlike commonMain); errors as Result/custom exceptions; Hilt constructor injection; fakes over mocks. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (Ktor/SQLDelight/Dispatchers.Default — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-interop); for the overview use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, modules android-modularization, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-modularization: Native-Android Gradle modularization (multi-module app structure) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android module boundaries: Gradle build files (build.gradle(.kts) with implementation/api project dependencies), an :app / :feature / :core / :data module, or navigation between features. Covers low coupling and high cohesion; the common module types (app/feature/data/core); the rule that feature modules never depend on other feature modules (the app module mediates, usually via the navigation graph); keeping each module's public surface minimal with Kotlin internal; preferring Gradle implementation over api to avoid leaking transitive deps; and passing primitive IDs (not whole objects) across boundaries. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain source-set layout (a different axis — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-structure); for in-app layering use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, repositories android-data-layer, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-ui-layer: Native-Android UI-layer state holders (ViewModel + UI state) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android ViewModel or screen-level state in an app/feature module (androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel / viewModelScope / StateFlow imports; keywords ViewModel, UiState, collectAsStateWithLifecycle, repeatOnLifecycle, main-safe). Covers the ViewModel as screen-level state holder (survives configuration changes, main-safe, holds NO View/Context/lifecycle reference); modeling UI state as one immutable data class (or a sealed UiState when states are genuinely exclusive); exposing it via read-only StateFlow; and consuming it lifecycle-aware via collectAsStateWithLifecycle (Compose) or repeatOnLifecycle (Views) so collection stops in the background. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); for the overview use android-architecture, repositories android-data-layer, Compose recomposition/side-effects jetpack-compose, Compose-MP UI kmp-compose-mp-ui, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:jetpack-compose: Native-Android Jetpack Compose UI discipline — load when reading/writing/reviewing @Composable code in a native-Android app/feature module (androidx.compose.* imports). Covers state hoisting (stateless composable, value down / events up); recomposition and stability (@Stable/@Immutable, stable params that let Compose skip, unstable collections, stable lambdas); the side-effect APIs (LaunchedEffect and its key restart, rememberCoroutineScope, DisposableEffect/onDispose, rememberUpdatedState, derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow, produceState); remember vs remember(key) vs rememberSaveable; stable keys for lazy-list items; modifier order and the modifier-parameter convention; slot APIs; previews/testing. Do NOT use for Compose Multiplatform / non-Android targets (Skia canvas, UIKitView, iOS/desktop/web — use kmp-compose-mp-ui) or KMP commonMain shared code (kmp-multiplatform); for the architecture overview use android-architecture, ViewModel/UI-state rules android-ui-layer, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:kmp-compose-mp-ui: Depth guidance for Compose Multiplatform UI across non-Android targets (iOS, desktop, web/Wasm). Covers the central fact that Compose MP renders via a Skiko/Skia canvas, not native UIKit/SwiftUI widgets, and what follows (identical look by default, native-view interop, simulated-native iOS scroll physics since 1.8.0, on-device verification of canvas/interop/accessibility); choosing Compose MP vs native UI per target; stability (iOS Stable since 1.8.0, desktop Stable, Web/Wasm Beta); resources, fonts, density; navigation. Use when building or reviewing shared Compose UI for iOS/desktop/web, deciding Compose MP vs SwiftUI/native, debugging gestures or scroll feel on iOS, handling images/fonts/strings, or wiring shared navigation. Trigger keywords — Compose Multiplatform, Skiko, desktop Compose, Compose for Web, Wasm, UIKitView, compose-resources, navigation. Do NOT use for Android-only Jetpack Compose, non-UI logic (use kmp-structure), or Swift/Kotlin interop (use kmp-interop).
- kotlin:kmp-interop: Depth guidance for Kotlin <-> Swift/Objective-C interop and per-platform networking in KMP. Covers refining the ObjC header Kotlin exports to Swift (@HiddenFromObjC, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift), why not to expose Flow directly to Swift (use SKIE) and that suspend->Swift async is officially experimental, exported-surface quirks (top-level funcs become <FileName>Kt classes, generics only on classes, no default args), and Ktor with ktor-client-core in commonMain plus an engine per platform (Darwin/OkHttp/CIO). Use when designing the API a Swift/iOS app consumes from shared Kotlin, debugging an awkward generated Swift signature, deciding how to bridge Flow or suspend to Swift, or wiring the Ktor client. Trigger keywords — Swift interop, Objective-C, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift, SKIE, Flow to Swift, suspend async, Ktor, Darwin, OkHttp. Do NOT use for shared logic structure (use kmp-structure), Compose UI (use kmp-compose-mp-ui), or everyday Kotlin language style (use kotlin-style).
- kotlin:kmp-multiplatform: Kotlin Multiplatform framework rules for shared code — load when reading, writing, or reviewing files under a commonMain or commonTest source set (auto-scoped to **/commonMain/**/*.kt and **/commonTest/**/*.kt), or on demand for KMP layout questions. Covers where shared code lives and the one-way platform->common dependency, what to share vs keep native, the commonMain-only coroutine constraint (Dispatchers.Default not IO, because IO is JVM/Native-only and breaks JS/Wasm), the expect/actual escalation ladder, and commonTest using kotlin.test only (no JUnit, which breaks Native). Keywords — KMP, multiplatform, commonMain, commonTest, expect, actual, source set, Dispatchers in common code, JS, Wasm. Do NOT use for native-Android-only code (there Dispatchers.IO is correct — use the android skills), everyday Kotlin language style (kotlin-style), source-set depth (kmp-structure), Compose-MP UI (kmp-compose-mp-ui), or Swift interop (kmp-interop).

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. - update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. 1	---
2	name: jetpack-compose
3	description: Jetpack Compose patterns for declarative UI, state management, theming, animations, and performance optimization.
4	---
5	
6	# Jetpack Compose Patterns
7	
8	Modern declarative UI patterns for Android.
9	
10	## State Management
11	
12	### State Hoisting
13	
14	```kotlin
15	// ✅ CORRECT: Stateless composable
16	@Composable
17	fun Counter(
18	    count: Int,
19	    onIncrement: () -> Unit,
20	    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
21	) {
22	    Row(modifier = modifier) {
23	        Text("Count: $count")
24	        Button(onClick = onIncrement) {
25	            Text("+")
26	        }
27	    }
28	}
29	
30	// Parent owns state
31	@Composable
32	fun CounterScreen() {
33	    var count by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(0) }
34	    
35	    Counter(
36	        count = count,
37	        onIncrement = { count++ }
38	    )
39	}
40	```
41	
42	### Remember Variants
43	
44	```kotlin
45	// remember - Survives recomposition
46	val alpha by remember { mutableStateOf(1f) }
47	
48	// rememberSaveable - Survives config change
49	var count by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(0) }
50	
51	// remember with key - Resets on key change
52	val animation = remember(itemId) { Animatable(0f) }
53	
54	// derivedStateOf - Computed, updates only when result changes
55	val isValid by remember {
56	    derivedStateOf { email.isNotBlank() && password.length >= 8 }
57	}
58	```
59	
60	## Composition Patterns
61	
62	### Slot API
63	
64	```kotlin
65	@Composable
66	fun AppBar(
67	    title: @Composable () -> Unit,
68	    navigationIcon: @Composable () -> Unit = {},
69	    actions: @Composable RowScope.() -> Unit = {}
70	) {
71	    TopAppBar(
72	        title = { title() },
73	        navigationIcon = { navigationIcon() },
74	        actions = actions
75	    )
76	}
77	
78	// Usage
79	AppBar(
80	    title = { Text("Home") },
81	    navigationIcon = { IconButton(onClick = {}) { Icon(Icons.Default.Menu, null) } },
82	    actions = {
83	        IconButton(onClick = {}) { Icon(Icons.Default.Search, null) }
84	    }
85	)
86	```
87	
88	### Modifier Pattern
89	
90	```kotlin
91	@Composable
92	fun CustomButton(
93	    onClick: () -> Unit,
94	    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,  // First optional parameter
95	    enabled: Boolean = true,
96	    content: @Composable RowScope.() -> Unit
97	) {
98	    Button(
99	        onClick = onClick,
100	        modifier = modifier,  // Apply modifier first
101	        enabled = enabled,
102	        content = content
103	    )
104	}
105	```
106	
107	## Side Effects
108	
109	### LaunchedEffect
110	
111	```kotlin
112	@Composable
113	fun HomeScreen(viewModel: HomeViewModel) {
114	    // Runs once
115	    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
116	        viewModel.loadData()
117	    }
118	    
119	    // Runs when key changes
120	    LaunchedEffect(userId) {
121	        viewModel.loadUser(userId)
122	    }
123	}
124	```
125	
126	### DisposableEffect
127	
128	```kotlin
129	@Composable
130	fun LifecycleObserver(onResume: () -> Unit) {
131	    val lifecycleOwner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current
132	    
133	    DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner) {
134	        val observer = LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
135	            if (event == Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME) onResume()
136	        }
137	        lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer)
138	        
139	        onDispose {
140	            lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.removeObserver(observer)
141	        }
142	    }
143	}
144	```
145	
146	## Theming
147	
148	### Material 3
149	
150	```kotlin
151	@Composable
152	fun AppTheme(
153	    darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(),
154	    content: @Composable () -> Unit
155	) {
156	    val colorScheme = if (darkTheme) DarkColorScheme else LightColorScheme
157	    
158	    MaterialTheme(
159	        colorScheme = colorScheme,
160	        typography = AppTypography,
161	        content = content
162	    )
163	}
164	
165	// Usage
166	val backgroundColor = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.surface
167	val textStyle = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyLarge
168	```
169	
170	## Lists
171	
172	### LazyColumn
173	
174	```kotlin
175	LazyColumn {
176	    items(
177	        items = users,
178	        key = { it.id }  // Critical for performance
179	    ) { user ->
180	        UserItem(user = user)
181	    }
182	}
183	```
184	
185	## Animations
186	
187	### Animate Values
188	
189	```kotlin
190	val alpha by animateFloatAsState(
191	    targetValue = if (visible) 1f else 0f,
192	    animationSpec = tween(durationMillis = 300)
193	)
194	
195	val size by animateDpAsState(
196	    targetValue = if (expanded) 200.dp else 100.dp
197	)
198	```
199	
200	### AnimatedContent
201	
202	```kotlin
203	AnimatedContent(
204	    targetState = state,
205	    transitionSpec = {
206	        fadeIn() togetherWith fadeOut()
207	    }
208	) { targetState ->
209	    when (targetState) {
210	        is Loading -> LoadingContent()
211	        is Success -> SuccessContent(targetState.data)
212	        is Error -> ErrorContent()
213	    }
214	}
215	```
216	
217	---
218	
219	**Remember**: Compose is declarative. Describe the UI, don't command it.
220

1	---
2	name: compose-animations
3	description: "Use when writing or reviewing Jetpack Compose motion: visibility enter/exit, animating one property toward a target, color or size transitions, multiple properties from one state, switching composable content, or choosing between AnimatedVisibility, animate*AsState, rememberTransition, AnimatedContent, and Crossfade."
4	---
5	
6	# Compose: animations
7	
8	## Core principle
9	
10	Pick the **smallest API that matches the problem**: built-in visibility and layout transitions first, then a single animated value, then a shared transition object when several values must move together, then gesture-level or imperative APIs when the framework cannot express the motion.
11	
12	## Review procedure
13	
14	1. Identify the visual job: show/hide, one value, coordinated values, content swap, size change, or gesture-driven motion.
15	2. Choose the smallest API from the table below.
16	3. Check lifecycle semantics: should hidden content leave composition, keep focus/state, or only become transparent?
17	4. Check identity: for state-holder wrappers, choose `AnimatedContent.contentKey` by visual shape rather than payload churn.
18	5. Check performance: keep frame-rate animation values as `State` and read them in layout/draw block modifiers when possible.
19	6. Escalate to `Animatable` or lower-level APIs only when target-state animation cannot express the motion.
20	
21	## Pick the smallest animation API
22	
23	| Need | API |
24	|---|---|
25	| Show or hide a subtree with enter/exit semantics; content is removed after exit completes | [`AnimatedVisibility`](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/composables-modifiers#animatedvisibility) |
26	| Animate one property toward a target derived from state | [`animateFloatAsState`](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/value-based#animate-as-state) / `animateDpAsState` / `animateColorAsState` / `animateOffsetAsState` / … |
27	| Several animated values keyed off one boolean, enum, or sealed state | `rememberTransition` + transition child animations (`animateFloat`, `animateDp`, `animateColor`, `animateValue`, …) |
28	| Smooth size when child layout height/width changes (e.g. text wraps) | `Modifier.animateContentSize()` |
29	| Swap between different composable trees for the same slot | `AnimatedContent` or `Crossfade` |
30	| User-driven motion (drag, fling, interruptible springs) | [`Animatable`](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/compose/animation/core/Animatable) and related coroutine APIs (see Advanced pointers) |
31	
32	## Appear and disappear
33	
34	**Prefer `AnimatedVisibility`** when the UI should leave or join the tree with enter/exit transitions.
35	
36	```kotlin
37	AnimatedVisibility(visible = expanded) {
38	    Text("Details…")
39	}
40	```
41	
42	**`animateFloatAsState` on alpha** only fades; the composable **stays in composition** and continues to participate in layout unless you gate it yourself. Use that tradeoff when you intentionally keep children mounted (state, focus) but visually hidden. For true remove-from-tree behavior, use `AnimatedVisibility` (or conditional composition with `AnimatedVisibility` / `AnimatedContent` patterns from the [quick guide](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/quick-guide)).
43	
44	## Background color
45	
46	Use `animateColorAsState` for smooth color targets.
47	
48	For animated fills behind children, the [quick guide](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/quick-guide) recommends drawing with **`Modifier.drawBehind`** rather than `Modifier.background()` so the animated color is applied in the draw phase appropriately for performance.
49	
50	```kotlin
51	val background = animateColorAsState(
52	    targetValue = if (selected) selectedColor else idleColor,
53	    label = "background",
54	)
55	Box(
56	    Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(background.value) },
57	) { /* content */ }
58	```
59	
60	## Size changes
61	
62	`Modifier.animateContentSize()` animates layout size changes—common for expanding/collapsing text or dynamic chips—without hand-rolling width/height animations.
63	
64	## Value-based animations (`animate*AsState`)
65	
66	Compose provides `animate*AsState` for `Float`, `Dp`, `Color`, `Size`, `Offset`, `Rect`, `Int`, `IntOffset`, `IntSize`, and more. You supply the **target**; the API owns the animation state.
67	
68	- Pass an [`AnimationSpec`](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/compose/animation/core/AnimationSpec) via `animationSpec` (e.g. `spring`, `tween`) when defaults are wrong for the UI.
69	- Set a distinct **`label`** for debugging and tooling when multiple animations exist in one composable.
70	- For completion or sequencing details, see [Value-based animations](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/value-based).
71	
72	```kotlin
73	val width by animateDpAsState(
74	    targetValue = if (expanded) 200.dp else 56.dp,
75	    animationSpec = spring(dampingRatio = 0.7f, stiffness = Spring.StiffnessMedium),
76	    label = "fabWidth",
77	)
78	```
79	
80	## Multiple properties: `rememberTransition`
81	
82	When one piece of state (e.g. `enum class Phase { A, B, C }`) should drive **several** animated values in lockstep, use `rememberTransition` and define child animations on that transition:
83	
84	```kotlin
85	val transition = rememberTransition(targetState = phase, label = "phase")
86	val alpha by transition.animateFloat(label = "alpha") { target ->
87	    if (target == Phase.Visible) 1f else 0f
88	}
89	val offset by transition.animateDp(label = "offset") { target ->
90	    if (target == Phase.Visible) 0.dp else 24.dp
91	}
92	```
93	
94	Avoid multiple independent `animate*AsState` calls that should stay visually synchronized but can drift if specs or targets diverge. Older code may use `updateTransition`; prefer `rememberTransition` for new code.
95	
96	## Choosing between content-level APIs
97	
98	Use the official [Choose an animation API](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/choose-api) tree when the table is not enough. Compressed rules:
99	
100	| Situation | Prefer |
101	|---|---|
102	| Same composable, different **target values** for layout properties | `animate*AsState` or `rememberTransition` |
103	| Different **composable content** for the same region (tabs, steps) | `AnimatedContent` (custom `transitionSpec`, `contentKey`) or simpler `Crossfade` |
104	| Pager-like **swipe between pages** | Horizontal pager APIs from the animation docs / Material—follow the choose-api guidance |
105	| Transitions **owned by Navigation Compose** | Use navigation’s built-in transitions rather than bolting `AnimatedContent` on top of the same destination swap |
106	
107	**Art-based motion** (illustrations, Lottie, complex vector timelines) is outside this skill; use dedicated libraries.
108	
109	## Decision flow (high level)
110	
111	```mermaid
112	flowchart TD
113	  start[Animation_need]
114	  start --> showHide{Show_or_hide_subtree}
115	  showHide -->|yes| av[AnimatedVisibility]
116	  showHide -->|no| oneProp{Single_property_to_target}
117	  oneProp -->|yes| asState["animate*AsState"]
118	  oneProp -->|no| multiProp{Many_props_one_state}
119	  multiProp -->|yes| rt[rememberTransition]
120	  multiProp -->|no| swapTree{Different_composable_content}
121	  swapTree -->|yes| ac[AnimatedContent_or_Crossfade]
122	  swapTree -->|no| advanced[Animatable_or_lower_level]
123	```
124	
125	## AnimatedContent keys for state holders
126	
127	When `AnimatedContent` receives a state-holder wrapper such as `AsyncResult<T>`, `Result<T>`, or a sealed `UiState`, decide what should actually trigger the transition. Usually the animation should run when the **content shape** changes (loading → content → error), not when the payload inside the same shape changes.
128	
129	Use `contentKey` to map rich state to the animation identity:
130	
131	```kotlin
132	AnimatedContent(
133	    targetState = result,
134	    contentKey = { state ->
135	        when (state) {
136	            AsyncResult.Loading -> "loading"
137	            is AsyncResult.Success -> "content"
138	            is AsyncResult.Error -> "error"
139	        }
140	    },
141	    label = "profile-content",
142	) { state ->
143	    when (state) {
144	        AsyncResult.Loading -> Loading()
145	        is AsyncResult.Success -> Profile(state.value)
146	        is AsyncResult.Error -> ErrorMessage(state.throwable)
147	    }
148	}
149	```
150	
151	Without `contentKey`, every unequal `Success(value)` can be treated as new content. That is useful if a payload change should animate, but noisy when fresh data updates the same screen shape.
152	
153	Choose keys by visual shape:
154	
155	| State change | Typical `contentKey` |
156	|---|---|
157	| Loading → Success → Error | Branch key: `"loading"`, `"content"`, `"error"` |
158	| Success item A → Success item B should crossfade | Stable item id |
159	| Success data refresh should update in place | Constant content key for `Success` |
160	| Error message text changes but error UI shape stays | Constant content key for `Error` |
161	
162	## Animated values and composition performance
163	
164	`animate*AsState` returns `State` that updates frequently. If that value feeds `Modifier.offset`, `Modifier.graphicsLayer`, scroll-adjacent layout, or other **frame-rate** paths, avoid reading it in the composable body with `by` and then passing it into value-form modifiers—use **deferred reads** (block modifiers, draw/ layout lambdas) instead. See [`compose-state-deferred-reads`](../compose-state-deferred-reads/SKILL.md).
165	
166	If recomposition counters spike during motion unrelated to bad stability, see [`compose-recomposition-performance`](../compose-recomposition-performance/SKILL.md).
167	
168	## Escalation points
169	
170	Load the official docs when one of these applies:
171	
172	| Need | Start with |
173	|---|---|
174	| API tree is still ambiguous | [Choose an animation API](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/animation/choose-api) |
175	| Gesture-driven, interruptible, or cancelable motion | [`Animatable`](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/compose/animation/core/Animatable), pointer input, decay |
176	| Infinite or repeating cycles | [`rememberInfiniteTransition`](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/compose/animation/core/rememberInfiniteTransition) |
177	| Seekable or test-controlled progress | [`SeekableTransitionState`](https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/compose/animation/core/SeekableTransitionState) and related APIs |
178	
179	## Common mistakes
180	
181	| Mistake | Fix |
182	|---|---|
183	| Fade with `animateFloatAsState(alpha)` but expect children to unmount | Use `AnimatedVisibility` or remove the subtree from composition when hidden |
184	| Three `animateDpAsState` calls that must stay in sync with one enum | One `rememberTransition` + child animations |
185	| Animated color on `Modifier.background` causing extra work | Prefer `drawBehind { drawRect(animatedColor) }` per quick guide |
186	| Chaining `LaunchedEffect` + manual `Animatable` for simple target animation | Prefer `animate*AsState` or `rememberTransition` unless gestures require `Animatable` |
187	| Ignoring Navigation’s own transitions | Use Nav APIs for destination transitions; do not duplicate with `AnimatedContent` for the same swap |
188	| `AnimatedContent(targetState = asyncResult)` animates on every data refresh | Add `contentKey` based on the visual shape or stable item identity |
189	
190	## When not to use this skill
191	
192	- **Side-effect timing** (`LaunchedEffect`, clicks launching work): use [`compose-side-effects`](../compose-side-effects/SKILL.md).
193	- **Deep performance tuning** of where snapshot state is read: use [`compose-state-deferred-reads`](../compose-state-deferred-reads/SKILL.md) as the primary reference.
194

1	---
2	name: compose-focus-navigation
3	description: Use when writing or reviewing Jetpack Compose UI for TV, keyboard, desktop, accessibility focus, D-pad navigation, FocusRequester, focusProperties, key events, or initial focus behavior.
4	---
5	
6	# Compose: focus navigation
7	
8	## Core principle
9	
10	Focus is stateful UI behavior. Make focus targets explicit, request focus after composition succeeds, and test navigation with the same input model users use: keyboard, D-pad, or remote keys.
11	
12	## When to use this skill
13	
14	Use this when UI:
15	
16	- Runs on TV, desktop, ChromeOS, keyboard-first Android, or remote-control devices.
17	- Uses `FocusRequester`, `focusRequester`, `focusProperties`, `onFocusChanged`, or key handlers.
18	- Needs initial focus, restored focus, directional navigation, or back/escape behavior.
19	- Has a carousel, grid, lazy list, menu, dialog, or modal with focus traps.
20	- Has tests asserting which item is focused.
21	
22	## Build focus targets deliberately
23	
24	Start with components that already participate in focus, then add only the focus hooks the behavior needs:
25	
26	| Need | Add |
27	|---|---|
28	| Normal button/text field/clickable focus | Nothing extra; use the focusable component |
29	| Programmatic initial/restored focus | `FocusRequester` + `Modifier.focusRequester(...)` |
30	| Visual or state reaction to focus changes | `Modifier.onFocusChanged { ... }` |
31	| Custom interactive surface that is not already focusable | `Modifier.focusable()` plus role/semantics as appropriate |
32	
33	For example, request and observe focus only when both behaviors are needed:
34	
35	```kotlin
36	val requester = remember { FocusRequester() }
37	
38	Button(
39	    onClick = onClick,
40	    modifier = Modifier
41	        .focusRequester(requester)
42	        .onFocusChanged { state -> isFocused = state.isFocused },
43	) {
44	    Text("Play")
45	}
46	```
47	
48	Prefer focusable components (`Button`, `TextField`, clickable/selectable surfaces) over manually adding `focusable()` to passive layout. Add manual focus only when the element is truly interactive or participates in navigation.
49	
50	## Request focus after composition
51	
52	Call focus requests from an effect, not from the composable body:
53	
54	```kotlin
55	val initialFocus = remember { FocusRequester() }
56	
57	LaunchedEffect(initialFocus) {
58	    initialFocus.requestFocus()
59	}
60	```
61	
62	If the target appears after loading, key the request to the condition:
63	
64	```kotlin
65	LaunchedEffect(items.isNotEmpty()) {
66	    if (items.isNotEmpty()) {
67	        firstItemRequester.requestFocus()
68	    }
69	}
70	```
71	
72	For lazy content, request focus only after the item is actually composed. Keep requesters in stable item state keyed by item id, not by index alone if the list can reorder.
73	
74	## Directional navigation
75	
76	Use `focusProperties` when default spatial search is wrong:
77	
78	```kotlin
79	Modifier.focusProperties {
80	    up = headerRequester
81	    down = firstRowRequester
82	    left = FocusRequester.Cancel
83	}
84	```
85	
86	Use this sparingly. Too many hard-coded links create stale focus graphs when layouts change. Prefer natural focus order unless the design requires a specific jump or trap.
87	
88	## Key events
89	
90	Use key handlers for behavior that is not normal click/focus traversal:
91	
92	```kotlin
93	Modifier.onPreviewKeyEvent { event ->
94	    if (event.type == KeyEventType.KeyUp && event.key == Key.Back) {
95	        onBack()
96	        true
97	    } else {
98	        false
99	    }
100	}
101	```
102	
103	Return `true` only when consumed. Returning `true` too broadly breaks text entry, accessibility shortcuts, and parent navigation.
104	
105	For rapid D-pad input, throttle at the boundary that owns the expensive behavior (for example row scrolling or paging), not globally across the whole screen.
106	
107	## Focus restoration
108	
109	Preserve focus by semantic identity:
110	
111	- Track selected/focused item id, not just index.
112	- Use stable `key` values in lazy lists and grids.
113	- When content refreshes, re-request focus for the same id if it still exists.
114	- If it no longer exists, choose a deterministic fallback: nearest neighbor, first item, or parent container.
115	
116	## Common mistakes
117	
118	| Mistake | Fix |
119	|---|---|
120	| Adding `focusRequester` and `onFocusChanged` to every button | Add them only when requesting or observing focus |
121	| `requestFocus()` in the composable body | Move to `LaunchedEffect` |
122	| Initial focus keyed to `Unit` while target appears later | Key to loaded/visible condition |
123	| Focus requesters stored by lazy list index | Store by stable item id |
124	| Everything gets custom `focusProperties` | Let spatial search work; override only broken edges |
125	| Key handler returns `true` for all keys | Consume only handled keys |
126	| Tests click nodes in TV/D-pad UI | Send key input and assert focus |
127	
128	## Testing
129	
130	Test focus through user input:
131	
132	```kotlin
133	composeTestRule.onNodeWithTag("screen").performKeyInput {
134	    pressKey(Key.DirectionDown)
135	}
136	
137	composeTestRule.onNodeWithTag("play-button").assertIsFocused()
138	```
139	
140	Prefer asserting focused semantics over visual styling. Use screenshot tests only for focus appearance, not for deterministic focus ownership.
141	
142	Broader test-shape choices (plain UI vs integration, semantics-first): [`compose-ui-testing-patterns`](../compose-ui-testing-patterns/SKILL.md).
143	
144	## Red flags during review
145	
146	- "It focuses correctly when I tap it" for a keyboard/TV UI.
147	- Initial focus works only with fixed data and fails after loading/refresh.
148	- Focus state is inferred from selected data state when focus and selection are different concepts.
149	- The focus graph is described in comments but not encoded or tested.
150

1	---
2	name: compose-modifier-and-layout-style
3	description: Use when writing or reviewing Jetpack Compose layout APIs, modifier parameters, modifier chain construction, hardcoded root layout decisions, or layout wrappers around a single conditional.
4	---
5	
6	# Compose modifier and layout style
7	
8	## Core principle
9	
10	A composable that emits layout is a leaf the *parent* places — the parent decides position, size, alignment, padding. The composable's job is structure (what's inside), not placement (where it goes). Three rules follow:
11	
12	- **Declare a `modifier` parameter and apply it to the root**, so the parent can actually do its job. Hardcoding `.fillMaxWidth()` on a composable's root takes that decision away from every future caller.
13	- **Construct modifier chains as one fluent expression**, not stepwise reassignments. Both compile to the same thing, but the chain *reads* as intent in one pass.
14	- **Conditional rendering belongs where the condition applies.** A layout call whose only content is one `if` exists solely to hold the condition — push the `if` outside instead.
15	
16	These travel together because the same composable usually triggers all three: you declare its parameters (rule 1), the caller constructs a chain to position it (rules 2), and the body has a conditional you might be tempted to wrap (rule 3).
17	
18	## When to use this skill
19	
20	- You're writing a `@Composable fun` that calls a layout (`Box`, `Column`, `Row`, `LazyColumn`, `Text`, `Image`, `Surface`, `Card`, `Layout { … }`, anything from `compose.foundation.layout` or `compose.material*`) and its signature has no `modifier` parameter, or has one that isn't applied to the root, or has a hardcoded `.fillMaxWidth()`/`.padding(...)` on the root.
21	- You see `var m = Modifier` followed by `m = m.padding(…)`, `m = m.background(…)`, etc.
22	- A `modifier = …` argument has three or more chained calls on a single line.
23	- A composable's body is `Layout { if (cond) Content() }` — one conditional, nothing else.
24	
25	## 1. Declare a `modifier` parameter
26	
27	For composables that emit layout, prefer a `modifier` parameter after required parameters and before content/lambda parameters, with a default of `Modifier`. The name is exactly `modifier` — not `mod`, not `m`, not `wrapperModifier`.
28	
29	```kotlin
30	// ❌ BAD — no modifier param; caller can't position, size, or constrain this
31	@Composable
32	fun HomeScreenHeader(title: String, subtitle: String) {
33	    Column(
34	        modifier = Modifier
35	            .fillMaxWidth()
36	            .padding(horizontal = 16.dp),
37	        verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(4.dp),
38	    ) {
39	        Text(title, style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineLarge)
40	        Text(subtitle, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium)
41	    }
42	}
43	```
44	
45	```kotlin
46	// ✅ GOOD — parent decides width and padding; the composable describes structure only
47	@Composable
48	fun HomeScreenHeader(
49	    title: String,
50	    subtitle: String,
51	    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
52	) {
53	    Column(
54	        modifier = modifier,
55	        verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(4.dp),
56	    ) {
57	        Text(title, style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineLarge)
58	        Text(subtitle, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium)
59	    }
60	}
61	```
62	
63	The caller now writes `HomeScreenHeader(title, subtitle, Modifier.fillMaxWidth().padding(horizontal = 16.dp))` once, at the home screen — the only place that knows the layout actually wants those.
64	
65	## 2. Apply the caller's modifier to the root, and apply it first
66	
67	When the root layout already takes other arguments (alignment, arrangement, padding *that's intrinsic to the composable*), the caller-provided modifier still goes on the root layout's `modifier` parameter — and the composable's local chain is appended after.
68	
69	```kotlin
70	// ❌ BAD — modifier accepted but never applied
71	@Composable
72	fun Avatar(url: String, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
73	    Image(painter = rememberAsyncImagePainter(url), contentDescription = null)
74	}
75	
76	// ❌ BAD — applied to a child, not the root; caller's size/position changes don't take
77	@Composable
78	fun Avatar(url: String, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
79	    Box {
80	        Image(
81	            painter = rememberAsyncImagePainter(url),
82	            contentDescription = null,
83	            modifier = modifier,
84	        )
85	    }
86	}
87	
88	// ❌ BAD — caller's modifier ends up last, so the composable's own size wins
89	@Composable
90	fun Avatar(url: String, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
91	    Image(
92	        painter = rememberAsyncImagePainter(url),
93	        contentDescription = null,
94	        modifier = Modifier
95	            .clip(CircleShape)
96	            .size(48.dp)
97	            .then(modifier),
98	    )
99	}
100	```
101	
102	```kotlin
103	// ✅ GOOD — caller's modifier first, then the composable's intrinsic chain
104	@Composable
105	fun Avatar(url: String, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
106	    Image(
107	        painter = rememberAsyncImagePainter(url),
108	        contentDescription = null,
109	        modifier = modifier
110	            .clip(CircleShape)
111	            .size(48.dp),
112	    )
113	}
114	```
115	
116	Order matters: in a modifier chain, the *earlier* segment is the outer wrapper. The caller's modifier should be the outermost so caller-provided `.size(...)` or `.padding(...)` can override the composable's defaults rather than being overridden by them.
117	
118	## 3. Don't hardcode layout decisions on the root
119	
120	If the composable's root has `.fillMaxWidth()`, `.padding(horizontal = 16.dp)`, `.height(56.dp)`, etc., the caller can't *not* have them. Those are layout choices the parent should own.
121	
122	```kotlin
123	// ❌ BAD — every caller now fills max width whether they want to or not
124	@Composable
125	fun PrimaryButton(text: String, onClick: () -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
126	    Button(
127	        onClick = onClick,
128	        modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth(),   // ← hardcoded
129	    ) { Text(text) }
130	}
131	
132	// ✅ GOOD — caller adds .fillMaxWidth() if (and only if) they want it
133	@Composable
134	fun PrimaryButton(text: String, onClick: () -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
135	    Button(onClick = onClick, modifier = modifier) { Text(text) }
136	}
137	```
138	
139	The carve-out is for modifiers that are part of the **identity** of the composable — what makes an `Avatar` an avatar (the `.clip(CircleShape)` and a default `.size(48.dp)`), not where it sits on the screen. Test: can you imagine a caller wanting a version of this composable *without* that modifier? If yes, push it out. If no (an avatar without `clip(CircleShape)` isn't an avatar), keep it — but put it *after* the caller's modifier in the chain (see §2).
140	
141	## 4. Construct modifier chains as one fluent expression
142	
143	Recomposition re-runs the composable body — every modifier expression is re-evaluated. Reassigning `var modifier =` step-by-step looks plausible but breaks the visual flow, invites further mutation, and produces nothing a chain doesn't.
144	
145	```kotlin
146	// ❌ BAD — visual flow broken into reassignments; `var` invites more mutation
147	@Composable
148	fun Demo() {
149	    var m = Modifier
150	    m = m.padding(16.dp)
151	    m = m.fillMaxSize()
152	    Box(m) { }
153	}
154	
155	// ❌ ALSO BAD — same shape, dressed up with .then()
156	@Composable
157	fun Demo() {
158	    var m = Modifier
159	    m = m.padding(16.dp)
160	    m = m.then(Modifier.fillMaxSize())
161	    Box(m) { }
162	}
163	```
164	
165	```kotlin
166	// ✅ GOOD
167	@Composable
168	fun Demo() {
169	    val m = Modifier
170	        .padding(16.dp)
171	        .fillMaxSize()
172	    Box(m) { }
173	}
174	```
175	
176	`val`, not `var`: once the chain is built, nothing should re-bind it. The reassignment shape is what makes `var` look necessary; the chain shape doesn't need it.
177	
178	### Inline at the call site is fine for short chains
179	
180	For one or two calls, build the modifier inline. The "extract to a `val`" rule only earns its keep when the chain is long enough to be worth naming, or when the same chain repeats.
181	
182	```kotlin
183	// ✅ GOOD — short chain inline
184	Box(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) { … }
185	Box(modifier = Modifier.padding(8.dp).background(Color.Red)) { … }
186	```
187	
188	### Conditional segments stay on the chain
189	
190	A common reason to reach for `var` is "the modifier depends on a condition." It doesn't — splice the condition inline:
191	
192	```kotlin
193	// ✅ GOOD — conditional inside the chain, still one expression
194	Box(
195	    modifier = Modifier
196	        .fillMaxWidth()
197	        .then(if (selected) Modifier.background(Color.Red) else Modifier),
198	)
199	```
200	
201	`Modifier` (the empty modifier) is the identity element for `.then` — it lets you keep the chain shape when one branch contributes nothing.
202	
203	## 5. Multiline formatting at the call site
204	
205	When a `modifier` argument's chain has **three or more** calls, format multiline with one call per line. Indent the chain so the dotted calls align beneath the value.
206	
207	```kotlin
208	// ❌ BAD — three+ calls on one line; hard to scan
209	Box(
210	    modifier = modifier.fillMaxSize().padding(16.dp).weight(1f),
211	)
212	
213	// ✅ GOOD
214	Box(
215	    modifier = modifier
216	        .fillMaxSize()
217	        .padding(16.dp)
218	        .weight(1f),
219	)
220	```
221	
222	One or two calls stay on a single line — the threshold is the call count, not the character count. If a single call has very long arguments, that's a different problem (extract a `val`, or shorten the arguments).
223	
224	This applies *only* to a parameter named `modifier`. Other fluent-style arguments aren't covered here.
225	
226	## 6. Hoist single conditionals out of the layout
227	
228	When a layout's *only* content is one `if`, the layout exists solely to "hold" the conditional. Move the `if` outside — the layout will only exist when it has something to show.
229	
230	```kotlin
231	// ❌ BAD — Column always emitted; only its inner content is conditional
232	@Composable
233	fun A() {
234	    Column {
235	        if (showHeader) {
236	            Text("Title")
237	            Text("Subtitle")
238	        }
239	    }
240	}
241	
242	// ✅ GOOD — Column only exists when it has content
243	@Composable
244	fun A() {
245	    if (showHeader) {
246	        Column {
247	            Text("Title")
248	            Text("Subtitle")
249	        }
250	    }
251	}
252	```
253	
254	The benefit isn't a performance win — the runtime handles both fine — it's that the second form *reads* as "header section, conditionally." The first reads as "always-on column that may or may not have content."
255	
256	### The carve-outs (and why)
257	
258	- **Layout carries visual semantics that aren't conditional.** When the layout call passes `modifier`, `contentAlignment`, `horizontalArrangement`, or `verticalAlignment`, those arguments describe the *container*, not the content. Hoisting the conditional either loses those (the container collapses with the content) or duplicates them into both branches. Leave it.
259	
260	  ```kotlin
261	  // ✅ KEEP AS-IS — modifier on the container is doing visible work
262	  @Composable
263	  fun A(modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
264	      Box(modifier = modifier) {
265	          if (something) {
266	              Text("Bleh1")
267	              Text("Bleh2")
268	          }
269	      }
270	  }
271	  ```
272	
273	- **There are siblings to the `if`.** The layout has other content; the `if` is just one piece. Hoisting either pulls the siblings out (changing the layout) or leaves a different shape behind. Leave it.
274	
275	- **`if … else …` with both branches contributing composables.** Both branches do work; nothing to hoist; the layout *is* the shared container.
276	
277	  ```kotlin
278	  // ✅ KEEP AS-IS — both branches contribute to the layout
279	  Box {
280	      if (something) Text("Hint") else innerTextField()
281	  }
282	  ```
283	
284	## 7. Measure-phase constraint decoration
285	
286	When composable A captures a size and composable B must match it, **do not read the captured size in B's composable body** (`Modifier.height(state.dp)`). That ties B to composition whenever the measurement state changes.
287	
288	Capture in a layout callback on A; apply on B inside `Modifier.layout` so only layout invalidates:
289	
290	```kotlin
291	fun Modifier.decorateMeasureConstraints(
292	    decorate: (Constraints) -> Constraints,
293	): Modifier = layout { measurable, incoming ->
294	    val constraints = decorate(incoming).constrain(incoming)
295	    val placeable = measurable.measure(constraints)
296	    layout(placeable.width, placeable.height) {
297	        placeable.placeRelative(0, 0)
298	    }
299	}
300	```
301	
302	```kotlin
303	// Hoisted at the common parent of both rows:
304	//   var anchorHeightPx by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
305	
306	// Measured row — write state only from onSizeChanged
307	RowAnchor(Modifier.onSizeChanged { size -> if (size.height != anchorHeightPx) anchorHeightPx = size.height })
308	
309	// Sibling rows — read anchorHeightPx only inside layout
310	RowSibling(
311	    Modifier.decorateMeasureConstraints { incoming ->
312	        if (anchorHeightPx > 0) {
313	            // Clamp to incoming bounds so the constraint never exceeds the parent's max.
314	            incoming.copy(minHeight = anchorHeightPx, maxHeight = anchorHeightPx)
315	        } else {
316	            incoming
317	        }
318	    },
319	)
320	```
321	
322	Use a composition-time fallback (fixed height) only while `anchorHeightPx` is `0`. See [`compose-state-deferred-reads`](../compose-state-deferred-reads/SKILL.md) for the full cross-row pattern.
323	
324	## Quick reference
325	
326	| Symptom | Diagnosis | Fix |
327	|---|---|---|
328	| `@Composable fun Foo(text: String)` with `Column`/`Box`/`Text` in body | No `modifier` param (§1) | Add `modifier: Modifier = Modifier`; pass to root |
329	| `modifier: Modifier = Modifier` declared but never referenced | Param ignored (§2) | Apply to root layout's `modifier` arg |
330	| `modifier` passed to a child, not the root | Wrong target (§2) | Move to the outermost layout's `modifier` |
331	| `modifier = Modifier.x().y().then(modifier)` | Caller's modifier last (§2) | Reorder: `modifier = modifier.x().y()` |
332	| `modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth().padding(...)` on a general-purpose component | Layout hardcoded (§3) | Remove the hardcoded calls; let callers add them |
333	| Sibling composables in the file don't have `modifier` either | Spreading anti-pattern | Fix this one; fix siblings opportunistically |
334	| `mod: Modifier = Modifier` or `wrapperModifier: Modifier = Modifier` | Wrong name (§1) | Rename to exactly `modifier` |
335	| `var m = Modifier` followed by `m = m.xxx()` reassignments | Stepwise modifier construction (§4) | One fluent chain on a `val`, or build inline |
336	| `var m = Modifier; m = m.then(Modifier.xxx())` | Same shape via `.then` (§4) | Collapse `.then(Modifier.x())` to `.x()` in the chain |
337	| Modifier branch needs a condition | Reaching for `var` (§4) | `.then(if (c) Modifier.x() else Modifier)` inside the chain |
338	| `modifier = modifier.a().b().c()` on one line | Long chain not formatted (§5) | One call per line, indented under the value |
339	| `Layout { if (cond) X() }` with no other content and no layout-tuning args | Hoist (§6) | Move the `if` outside the layout |
340	| `Box(modifier = …) { if (cond) X() }` | Layout carries semantics — leave (§6 carve-out) | Keep as-is |
341	| `Box { if (cond) X() else Y() }` | Both branches contribute — leave (§6 carve-out) | Keep as-is |
342	| Sibling lazy row reads `height(state)` from another row's measurement | Composition-time size coupling (§7) | Capture on measured row; apply via `decorateMeasureConstraints` on siblings |
343	
344	## When NOT to apply
345	
346	- **Composables that don't emit layout.** A `@Composable fun computeColor(): Color` or a `@Composable @ReadOnlyComposable` accessor doesn't emit a layout node. No `modifier` parameter needed (and a `@ReadOnlyComposable` couldn't accept one — see `compose-state-authoring`).
347	- **`@Preview` functions.** Previews are throwaway entry points; the framework calls them with no caller. A `modifier` parameter would be unused dead weight.
348	- **Test-only composables** inside `*Test` sources whose only caller is `composeTestRule.setContent { … }`. Same reasoning as previews.
349	- **Internal layout primitives that take a `modifier` as their *first required* parameter** (very rare; framework-level). The rule is "first *optional* param"; some private utilities legitimately have `modifier` upfront as required.
350	- **Modifier assembled imperatively from animation state.** A modifier built by appending values from `Animatable` or other procedural sources may legitimately need intermediate variables. The chain isn't the goal; readability is. If the chain becomes a worse expression, write the imperative form.
351	- **Slot APIs that store modifiers** in a data class or builder (rare; usually framework-level code). The fluent-chain idea is about user-site construction.
352	- **Test composables** pinning specific recomposition shapes — usually fine either way; don't refactor test composables purely for style.
353	
354	The declaration-side rules (§1–§3) should not be skipped merely because "this composable is internal", "only used in one place", "I'd rather not have the extra parameter on the signature", or "we know all the callers already". Those are exactly the rationalisations that produce composables that become single-use the day someone wants to call them twice.
355	
356	## Red flags during review
357	
358	| Thought | Reality |
359	|---|---|
360	| "This composable is internal-only — adding `modifier` is over-engineering" | The parameter is eight characters and a default. It's not over-engineering; it's the convention. Skipping it is the over-engineering — it's a custom decision against the grain of every Compose API. |
361	| "It's only used in one place, so I know the layout requirements" | "Only used in one place" describes today. The cost of the parameter is paid once; the cost of refactoring callers when the second use site appears is paid per caller. |
362	| "The sibling composables in this file don't have `modifier` either, so I'm matching style" | Spreading an anti-pattern isn't matching style. Fix this one. Fix the siblings opportunistically. |
363	| "The parent always wants `.fillMaxWidth()` here" | Then the parent passes `.fillMaxWidth()`. The composable doesn't decide that for callers it hasn't met yet. |
364	| "I'll add it when someone needs it" | You're someone. You need it now (for the convention). The next caller won't add it either — they'll work around its absence. |
365	| "It's a tiny composable — the modifier param is noise" | The param is eight characters at the declaration and zero characters at any call site that doesn't need it. The "noise" is imagined. |
366	| "I added `modifier` but kept `.fillMaxWidth()` on the root so the home screen doesn't have to" | Then the *not*-home-screen caller can't unset it. Move the `.fillMaxWidth()` to the caller. |
367	| "I need `var` for the modifier because the chain depends on a condition" | A conditional segment is `.then(if (c) Modifier.x() else Modifier)`, still on one chain. No `var` needed. |
368	| "Three lines is too few to make multiline" | Three chained calls *is* the threshold. Below three, one line. At or above three, multiline. |
369	| "The Column adds nothing but I'll keep it for symmetry" | Then hoist the conditional and keep the Column inside the consequent — symmetry preserved, no always-on container. |
370	| "I'll put the `if` inside because the layout already exists" | "Already exists" is the bug. The layout shouldn't exist when the condition is false. |
371	
372	## Related
373	
374	- [`compose-slot-api-pattern`](../compose-slot-api-pattern/SKILL.md) — the other half of declaring a reusable composable's public API: take `@Composable () -> Unit` slots for variable content. A reusable component takes both a `modifier` parameter *and* slots — caller owns placement *and* what to place.
375	- [`compose-state-deferred-reads`](../compose-state-deferred-reads/SKILL.md) — back-writing across phases and deferred measurement reads.
